claims.text: The starting material is a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy with a single-phase solid-solution microstructure.
Approximately 1 wt% Y2O3 is an effective oxide-addition level for this titanium- and nickel-containing alloy.
Mechanical alloying or high-energy ball milling can incorporate oxide dispersoids into a metal matrix.
Combined mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering can produce consolidated high-entropy-alloy samples with a fine-grained microstructure.
Spark plasma sintering at approximately 1000 °C is an appropriate consolidation condition for the proposed Y2O3-modified titanium- and nickel-containing alloy.
Optimized high-energy ball milling followed by SPS will produce a uniform nanometer-scale Y2O3 dispersion in the target alloy.
The Y2O3 particles will be located both along grain boundaries and within grains.
Dispersed Y2O3 nanoparticles will strengthen the alloy by oxide dispersion strengthening.
The Y2O3 nanoparticles will pin grain boundaries.
The Y2O3 nanoparticles will impede dislocation motion.
Grain-boundary pinning will retard grain coarsening during elevated-temperature exposure.
The oxide dispersion will reduce high-temperature creep deformation.
Y2O3 addition will increase elevated-temperature yield strength relative to an otherwise equivalent alloy without Y2O3.
Y2O3 addition will improve creep resistance relative to an otherwise equivalent alloy without Y2O3.
The intervention will improve overall high-temperature stability.
The predicted benefit applies during cyclic testing at 800–1000 °C in an oxidizing environment.
Non-uniform nanoparticle dispersion will reduce the strengthening effect.
The unmodified alloy has inferior high-temperature mechanical performance.
The exact magnitude of improvement depends on achieving an optimal and uniform nanoparticle distribution.

contradictions.description: The starting material is described as conventionally powder-metallurgy processed, whereas the experimental control is to be processed identically to the intervention by refined ball milling and SPS except for Y2O3. These are potentially different baselines, so the intended comparator is not consistent.

The modified material is said to contain a distinct dispersed Y2O3 phase while the boundary says the alloy must maintain a single-phase structure. This is contradictory unless 'single phase' is explicitly restricted to the metallic matrix.
